item.title: Structure-Aware Quantum Circuit Equivalence Checking via Sparse Pauli Propagation
item.description:
Skim new method — Framework gives reference-consistent equivalence decisions for 96.3% of 434 scored quantum circuit pairs up to 512 qubits with zero incorrect verdicts, cutting total runtime by 48.5%--76.0% relative to baselines.

Grade 0.524 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Tackling the Qubit Mapping Problem for NISQ-Era Quantum Devices”

Figure

The equivalence checking architecture, showing circuit routing between generator propagation and Cut-Miter backends based on rotation counts, accompanied by error-bounded certification.

Asks

How can equivalence checking of unitary quantum circuits avoid intermediate representation blowups caused by committing to a single symbolic representation or propagation strategy?

Before

Evaluated baselines achieved at most 68.7% reference-consistent decisions on the same 434 scored pairs.

But

Restricted to unitary quantum circuits; does not support mid-circuit measurements, classical feedforward control, dynamic reset, or non-trivial initial qubit layouts.

Tools

sparse Pauli propagation · generator propagation · Cut-Miter verification · Pauli-term pruning · bounded portfolio routing

Abstract

Quantum circuit equivalence checking is essential for validating compiler optimizations, but its computational cost can vary substantially with circuit structure. We present a structure-aware equivalence checker for unitary quantum circuits based on sparse Pauli propagation. It combines two complementary verification strategies: generator propagation compares the conjugation actions of the circuits on Pauli generators, while Cut-Miter exploits cancellation between circuit products at selected cut points. A structure-aware verification procedure uses circuit characteristics to select between these strategies while explicitly accounting for numerical and approximation errors. We evaluate our framework against three existing equivalence checkers on two benchmark suites containing circuit pairs with up to 512 qubits. Across 434 scored circuit pairs, our framework produces reference-consistent decisions for 96.3% of the pairs without any incorrect verdicts, while the evaluated baselines achieve at most 68.7% reference-consistent decisions. It also achieves the lowest aggregate runtime among the evaluated tools, reducing total runtime by 48.5%--76.0% relative to these baselines. Ablation studies confirm the benefits of cut-based verification, Pauli-term pruning, and bounded propagation attempts. These results indicate that structure-aware sparse Pauli propagation, combined with complementary verification strategies and explicit error accounting, can provide an effective approach to practical quantum circuit equivalence checking.

item.title: Improved Low-Cost Quantum Error Mitigation with Benchmarked-Noise Zero-Noise Extrapolation (bnZNE)
item.description:
Skim incremental — Randomized bnZNE improves mean expectation value fidelity ℱ over standard ZNE across multiple benchmark applications on 156-qubit IBM and 54-qubit IQM chips, often keeping mean error under 5%.

Grade 0.481 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers”

Figure

Mean single-qubit fidelity ℱ across six hardware applications on ibm_fez, comparing standard ZNE to bnZNE against the exact expectation value.

Asks

Can digital zero-noise extrapolation be improved for equal shot cost by using classically simulable benchmark circuits to directly measure effective error rates when running randomized circuits per noise level?

But

Increased variance in bnZNE estimates relative to ZNE as circuit depth grows; seven datapoints excluded where 3σ>1.5 in correlation decay fits; requires 2× circuit executions to run benchmark circuits.

Tools

ibm_fez (156-qubit Heron r2) · IQM Emerald (54-qubit device) · Pauli twirling · TREX readout error mitigation · circuit folding

Abstract

We theoretically extend and experimentally demonstrate benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE), a simple and low-cost method for quantum error mitigation which aims to outperform the highly popular ZNE method for an equal total shot cost by improving the classical extrapolation step. We recently proposed bnZNE as a new error mitigation method (Harris et al., arXiv:2603.10224 (2026)) and showed that it can mitigate noise to the same order as standard ZNE under gate-wise depolarizing noise. Here, we introduce randomized bnZNE which addresses the case of running multiple random circuits per noise level, allowing for the incorporation of noise-tailoring techniques like Pauli twirling and readout error mitigation, and test the method on the IBM and IQM hardware for a plethora of large-scale applications, observing bnZNE to consistently produce more accurate results than standard ZNE. Our approach enhances the extrapolation process to the zero-noise limit by using classically-simulable and structure-mirroring benchmark circuits, generated from the standard application circuit, to sensitively measure the effective error rate at each scaled noise level beyond simple integer values. We give a new method for generating tailored benchmark circuits for the IQM superconducting devices and test them experimentally. Our results demonstrate that bnZNE presents a versatile alternative to ZNE which can enable more accurate results at utility scales with an equivalent cost.
